It might actually be more. As of 2012 there are 644 million websites. Assuming each one has its own DNS entry, thats 644 million lines in the hosts file with the URL and corresponding ip addresses (plural because some have a DNS based load balancer).

Ever look at a log file that had over half a trillion lines? Shits pretty big.

assuming an average of 20 bytes per line:

600e6*20/1024/1024/1024 = 11.17GB. It's not nothing, but it also isn't 500GB. If we had something like easylist (all common sites) for this it would probably be more like 10MB

Twenty bytes is way too short:

  1. A full size IP address is fifteen characters(three sets of three numbers, plus three dots).

  2. There must be a space between the IP and the domain. That's an extra byte.

  3. Since the TLD is required, we need a dot between it and the domain name proper. There's another byte.

  4. We also need a newline. On UNIX and Mac systems, this is a single character, but Windows uses a two character sequence.

That means, from the guaranteed overhead alone, you have 18 or 19 bytes taken up. If we ignore the possibility that non-classical TLDs change the average, we also have three bytes right there. Assuming that the average domain name is eight ASCII characters long and that any subdomains are four characters long(based on 'www.'), that nets us:

Windows:

600e6 * 36 / 1024 / 1024 / 1024 = 20.12 GB

UNIX/Mac:

600e6 * 35 / 1024 / 1024 / 1024 = 19.56 GB

However, this is almost certainly a drastic underestimate for the following reasons:

  1. Despite being two characters long, many ccTLDs require a sub-TLD be used(eg, '.co.uk'), making them considerably larger in the hosts file.

  2. The new TLDs can be of any arbitrary length. Almost all are over three letters long.

  3. Most subdomains are longer than three letters(eg, 'mail.', 'store.').

  4. Unicode is now legal to use in the domain name and top level domain. That means a single character can take up up to four bytes.

Even if we ignore the size on disk, a file that large would drastically slow down performance since something that size will see constant cache misses on any home setup, making for shit performance system-wide. Then there's the problem of synchronizing it, which puts us back at square one.

You type in example.com. Your computer calls up a known DNS server to figure out example.com's IP address. Then it can find the right host to dial up and get that website's data.

These alternatives mean you change which DNS server your computer looks up to get example.com's IP. There is still the problem that a registrar takes over example.com though and just propagates its DNS record without a matching IP. These alternative DNS servers get around this by having their own ".com" extensions. Things you never heard of like example.bbs or example.chan.

So basically, change DNS servers so you can access new domain names that aren't in control by asshole registrars. The downside is only people who make this change can see example.bbs, so 99.99% of people can't visit example.bbs.
